body_paragraphs: Sunday closes out a week that spent five days promising escalation and one morning promising the opposite. Trump told his Cabinet at Camp David Friday that new strikes on Iran were coming 'as soon as this weekend'; by Sunday morning he'd cancelled them, citing an agreed framework to reopen the Strait of Hormuz after calls with Saudi Arabia's crown prince and pressure from Qatar, the UAE, Turkey, and Pakistan. Iran's own state media hasn't confirmed any of it, and Fars dismissed Trump's terms as a 'wish list.' Five months in, that gap between announcement and confirmation is the pattern worth remembering, not the announcement itself.

The market's read on all of it stayed unbothered through Friday's close - the S&P and Nasdaq extended their rally on Amazon's ~13% earnings surge, even as the 10-year topped 4.70% for the first time since January 2025. With markets shut all weekend, the next real test isn't the Iran headline but Friday's July jobs report, against Kalshi odds now favoring a September hike over a hold for the first time this cycle.

Locally, three clocks are running out at once: the Marlins - winners of six of their last seven - have about a day left before Monday's trade deadline decides Otto Lopez's summer; early voting opens tomorrow on Marine Stadium's restoration referendum; and Terra's marina application for the old Seaquarium site, 325 slips and a 500-boat dry stack, is now public alongside it. The Dolphins, by contrast, just opened camp to the public for the first time this season - a rare story this week with nothing left to decide.

The throughline: most of this week's biggest stories are open questions dressed as settled ones - worth treating this morning's calm as provisional, not resolved. Two housekeeping notes: no mobile feedback came in this week, so nothing below was starred by you, and this run couldn't reach the private notes that normally track your reading - so nothing was learned or adjusted either. Both resume once that connection is back.

themes.title: Trump cancels planned Iran strikes, citing a deal 'rapidly' coming together on Hormuz - Iran hasn't confirmed
themes.thesis: After a week of escalating threats culminating in a promise of imminent new strikes, Trump abruptly calls them off, claiming the outline of a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz - but Tehran's own state media gives no sign it agrees.
themes.synthesis: Trump told reporters he cancelled a planned attack on Iran after Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and other regional leaders - Qatar, the UAE, Turkey, Pakistan - pressed for de-escalation, and said the 'perimeters of a deal' had been agreed, centered on the immediate, total reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and an end to Iran's nuclear ambitions. Iranian state media gave no indication Tehran had requested the halt or changed its position on the strait, and the Fars news agency, close to Iran's Revolutionary Guard, dismissed Trump's terms as a 'wish list.' The war, five months old since the February 28 assassination of Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, has followed this shape before: a announced pause that doesn't survive confirmation.
themes.new_today: Trump's cancellation announcement, the claimed deal framework on Hormuz, MBS's Saturday call with Trump, and Iran's non-confirmation via Fars.
themes.why_it_matters: This is the most consequential of the war's several 'pauses' so far because it comes with an actual claimed framework, not just a quiet night - but the pattern all week was promise-then-reversal, and this is a promise from only one side of the conflict. Directly upstream of the oil and rate exposure running through the rest of this edition.

themes.title: Virginia Key's public waterfront faces two decisions this week - superyachts at the old Seaquarium, a rebuilt Marine Stadium
themes.thesis: Two separate decisions about the same stretch of public waterfront - the shuttered Seaquarium's marina redevelopment and Marine Stadium's management referendum - both reach key moments in the same week.
themes.synthesis: The Seaquarium closed in October 2025 after 70 years; developer David Martin's Terra Group bought the lease for $22.5 million and has applied to build what could be Miami-Dade's largest marina - 325 slips (about 90 for yachts over 80 feet), a 500-boat dry stack, a fuel depot, and floating docks extending partway across the channel - alongside a Fishermen's Village-style restaurant district and public baywalk. Environmental regulators have raised concerns about wetlands, coral, and water quality; if approved, demolition could begin late 2026 with an opening target around 2029. A short distance away, early voting opens tomorrow, August 3, on Referendum #172, a 40-year deal letting Global Spectrum/Oak View Group and Breakwater Hospitality manage a restored Marine Stadium; the city would keep 93% of event revenue and 85% of sponsorship income, with $10 million upfront and a separate $65-85 million restoration bond to follow. The vote is August 18.
themes.new_today: First dedicated coverage of the Seaquarium marina application's specific scope, and the start of early voting on the Marine Stadium referendum.
themes.why_it_matters: Two very different visions for public waterfront access, decided within weeks of each other on the same peninsula - worth tracking together for anyone who cares how Miami's shoreline gets used.

themes.title: The same leaf shape, evolved four different ways: what Darwin's daisies show about how evolution repeats itself
themes.thesis: Convergent evolution turns out to run on different genetic engines even within one small island chain - a tidy rebuttal to the idea that evolution has just one way of solving a given problem.
themes.synthesis: Scalesia, the Galapagos' giant daisies, independently evolved similar lobed, heat-tolerant leaf shapes across multiple lineages adapted to hot, dry lowlands and humid highland forests alike. A new Nature Communications study finds that while the outward leaf forms converged, the underlying genetic changes did not - each lineage arrived at a comparable shape through a distinct combination of genes rather than one shared pathway. Every Scalesia species alive today emerged within roughly the last million years.
themes.new_today: First dedicated coverage of the Nature Communications findings in this edition.
themes.why_it_matters: Appreciation-worthy with zero urgency attached - a genuine counterweight after a week of deadlines, and an echo of an idea worth sitting with: that similar-looking outcomes are often built from underneath in entirely different ways.

themes.title: How a fight to save pastel hotels in the 1970s became the reason Ocean Drive looks the way it does
themes.thesis: Miami Beach's Art Deco district survived not by accident but because a handful of preservationists fought developers who wanted the whole strip torn down for high-rises.
themes.synthesis: Miami Beach's building boom after the 1926 hurricane and through the Depression produced 'Tropical Deco' and later Streamline Moderne architecture - pastel facades, porthole windows, ocean-liner motifs - concentrated on Ocean Drive. By the 1970s, developers wanted much of it demolished for condo towers; Barbara Baer Capitman and the Miami Design Preservation League fought to save it instead. On May 14, 1979, the Miami Beach Architectural District became the first 20th-century urban district listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
themes.new_today: First dedicated coverage of the preservation history in this edition, as background to tonight's beautiful thing.
themes.why_it_matters: A local counterweight to a week of records and deadlines - the district that gives Miami Beach its look exists because people organized to keep it, not because nobody ever wanted to tear it down.

beautiful_thing.title: The Colony Hotel
beautiful_thing.creator: Henry Hohauser, architect
beautiful_thing.body: Henry Hohauser designed the Colony with fifty rooms, each with its own private bathroom, and features unusual for the time: a fireproof basement level with recreation and card rooms, and a rooftop solarium. Completed in 1935, it's considered the first true 'streamlined' building on Ocean Drive, establishing the Streamline Moderne look that other Miami Beach architects then adopted across the district. It later became a hub for musicians in the 1960s and '70s, hosting guests including Frank Sinatra, Dean Martin, and Sammy Davis Jr.

noticing_prompt.text: Notice how much of this week's news was stated as fact before it was actually a fact - a strike 'coming,' then cancelled; a deal whose 'perimeters' are agreed but whose other side hasn't spoken. What are you calling settled today that isn't?

daily_puzzle.prompt: A landlord raises a tenant's rent by 20%, then - stung by the pushback - cuts the new rent by 20%. Is the tenant now paying more than the original rent, less, or exactly the same? By how much?
daily_puzzle.hint: Try it with a real number, like $1,000, rather than reasoning about the percentages in the abstract.
daily_puzzle.solution: The tenant pays less - 4% less than the original rent. $1,000 raised 20% is $1,200; $1,200 cut 20% is $960.
daily_puzzle.explanation: The two 20% moves aren't mirror images, because the second percentage is taken from a different, larger base than the first.

threads.current_state: Trump says he's cancelled a planned new wave of strikes on Iran, citing an agreed framework - the immediate reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and an end to Iran's nuclear threat - after Saudi Arabia's MBS and other regional leaders pressed for de-escalation. Iranian state media has not confirmed any of it, and Iran's Fars news agency called Trump's terms a 'wish list.' The war remains five months old since the February 28 assassination of Ali Khamenei.

timeline.summary: First tracked: nine nights of US strikes, oil up about 20% this month, 10-day ceasefire being mediated.
10-day ceasefire formally proposed; US strikes continue, Iran calls it full-scale war, Brent tops $91, war cost estimated at $37.5B.
By Wednesday, strikes reach an eleventh consecutive night; Brent pushes past $92, reviving inflation concern.

Ceasefire proposal remains unadopted; Brent closes at $94.13, a five-week high; Strait transits fall to 25 ships from a peak of 49; Saudi coalition vows a forceful response to the Houthi blockade threat.
13th consecutive night of strikes; Iran hits Kuwait and the Houthis strike two Saudi tankers; Brent crosses $100 for the first time since May; Trump considers a massive attack.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard launches a fresh drone attack on Kuwait; sirens sound across Bahrain, Kuwait, and Qatar; Iran rejects an Iraqi-mediated ceasefire proposal; Brent holds near $100.

US carries out no new strikes overnight for the first time since the ceasefire collapsed; an Omani delegation arrives in Tehran to discuss Strait of Hormuz shipping; Brent eases to about $96.80, down nearly 4% but still up over 12% on the week.

Iran-aligned Houthi rebels fire dozens of ballistic missiles and drones at Saudi Aramco facilities in Jizan and Yanbu, starting large fires; read as retaliation for Saudi strikes on a Houthi-held Yemeni coastal city.

The pause holds through the weekend into Monday with no new strikes reported on either front; Brent tumbles toward the mid-$80s, down roughly 7% on the session, as Trump signals openness to renewed talks with Tehran.

Trump and Netanyahu meet at the White House for the first time since the war began, calling the talks 'positive and productive' and reaffirming a shared commitment against an Iranian nuclear weapon; Brent eases further into the mid-to-high $80s.

Iran says it struck US bases in Jordan and other Gulf locations overnight; Trump vows to hit back hard and repeats a bridge-bombing threat; the US and Saudi Arabia strike Iran-backed groups in Iraq; Brent jumps back above $90.

The US launches a 'heavy wave' of new strikes on Iran; Iranian state media reports at least three civilians killed. Iran retaliates against Jordan and Kuwait, killing a worker at a Chinese-owned building in Kuwait. Trump says it is now 'our turn' to hit Iran hard.
Qatar formally condemns Iran's strikes on Jordan and Kuwait as violations of sovereignty - the first significant regional diplomatic reaction against Tehran this round.

Iran's army claims strikes on US assets at Kuwait's Ahmad al-Jaber Air Base and Bahrain's Sheikh Isa Air Base; neither government confirms it. The US conducts no fresh strikes overnight - the first pause since Wednesday's heavy wave.

Egypt reports a drone of unknown origin hit two gas vessels at its Damietta port, a possible first sign the conflict is pulling in a new country; Brent eases 1.4% to $87.78 as Hormuz tanker traffic shows tentative recovery.

Kuwait's army confirms it intercepted a fresh wave of Iranian drones aimed at a government facility and civilian vehicles, the attack Iran claimed Thursday and nobody had confirmed. A tanker is hit by an unidentified projectile near Oman.

At Camp David, Trump says the US is planning new strikes on Iran 'as soon as this weekend'; only 28% of Americans approve of his handling of the five-month-old war. Brent back above $90, WTI near $84.67.

threads.title: Marlins wild card race
threads.current_state: Miami beat the Mets 6-2 Saturday on home runs from Javier Sanoja and Griffin Conine, its sixth win in seven games. Otto Lopez - hitting near .330 with career highs in hits and doubles and his first All-Star selection - remains in trade talks with the Red Sox and Guardians, with insider Jon Morosi still putting the odds of a deal at roughly 25%. The deadline is 6pm ET Monday, August 3.

timeline.summary: Hit the break 52-45, holding WC pole position.
Swept in Milwaukee; three straight losses out of the break.
Lost Astros opener; Meyer placed on IL with neck strain; streak at seven.
Lost again, confirmed final Houston 5, Miami 3; streak reaches eight straight, longest since April 2024.
Alcantara's start ends in a 5-2 loss; Houston completes the sweep; streak reaches nine straight.
Lost to the Padres 4-2 Friday night, the 10th straight loss, first time since June 2011; Miami falls to 52-52, first .500 record since June 19.
Lost again, 7-2, Ty France driving in three for San Diego; the streak reaches 11, tying the franchise record last matched in June 2011.

Lost Sunday 5-3 to San Diego, Machado and Merrill homering in the eighth to erase a three-run deficit; the streak reaches 12, an outright franchise record. Miami falls to 52-53, its first losing record since mid-June.

Miami beats the Phillies 8-7 on a walk-off single by Griffin Conine after Philadelphia's closer loaded the bases in the ninth, ending the losing streak at 12 - the Marlins' first win since July 9. Record moves to 53-53.

Correction: the 8-7 walk-off was Monday's game, not Tuesday's. Tuesday was a separate 1-0 win, Alcantara's major-league-leading 16th quality start with a Kyle Stowers homer; Miami has won two straight and stands 54-54 ahead of today's series finale.
Trade deadline plan surfaces: Miami will keep Alcantara, Eury Perez, Max Meyer, and Joe Mack, but is willing to take calls on Xavier Edwards, Otto Lopez, Liam Hicks, and Heriberto Hernandez.

Down 6-0, Miami completes the sweep of the Phillies with an 8-6 win, its biggest comeback of the season; Conine's go-ahead pinch-hit homer and two RBIs each from Lopez, Hernandez, and Edwards. Miami improves to 55-54, three straight wins, opening at the Mets next.

Deadline plan detail expands: Miami could also field calls on veteran relievers 31 or older - Anthony Bender, Michael Petersen, Lake Bachar, and John King - alongside the position-player names already in play, four days before the August 3 deadline.
Mets beat Miami 4-2 on Luis Robert Jr.'s eighth-inning two-run single, snapping Miami's three-game winning streak.

Boston reportedly weighs a bigger package for Otto Lopez that could include catcher Liam Hicks, after a wrist injury sidelines Red Sox infielder Curtis Mead for 6-8 weeks; Miami remains in a 'listening' stage rather than committed to a deal, three days before the deadline.
Miami beats the Mets 5-2, improving to 56-55 and staying in wild-card contention.

The Guardians join Boston in showing interest in Otto Lopez; insider Jon Morosi puts the odds of a trade at roughly 25%, with most signals pointing toward Miami keeping him, two days before the deadline.
Miami beats the Mets again, 6-2, on homers from Javier Sanoja and Griffin Conine - its sixth win in seven games, one day before the deadline.

threads.title: Dolphins rebuild under Hafley
threads.current_state: Today's practice - the fourth of camp - is the first open to the public this season, part of the NFL's 'Back Together Weekend,' free to fans and starting at 9:30am. It showcases new additions including quarterback Malik Willis and rookies Kadyn Proctor, Chris Johnson, Jacob Rodriguez, and Chris Bell, alongside the returning core: Willie Gay Jr.'s pick-six, Austin Jackson's recovery, Achane back after offseason shoulder surgery. Chris Bell remains on PUP. The next public dates are a Hard Rock Stadium practice August 8 and a joint practice with the Giants August 20; camp runs through August 26.

timeline.summary: Camp schedule announced.
Rookies reported; camp officially underway.
Jordyn Brooks signs three-year, $51.3M extension through 2029.
Joint-practice schedule confirmed: Aug. 12 at Washington, Aug. 20 hosting the Giants.
Veterans confirmed to report Tuesday, July 28; camp runs through Aug. 26 with the first public practice Aug. 2.
Veterans report as scheduled; training camp officially opens with the full squad on the field for the first time under Hafley.

First full practice: all veterans pass conditioning test; Achane fully participates after offseason shoulder surgery; Willie Gay Jr. sets an energetic tone; Chris Bell remains on PUP with no timetable.

Fuller Day One reporting: Willie Gay Jr.'s standout play was a one-handed interception returned for a touchdown off Cam Miller; Austin Jackson says he feels 'better than my normal self' after last year's rushed return from a toe injury.
Rookie safety Michael Taaffe intercepts backup quarterback Quinn Ewers, his former Texas teammate, in team drills.
Edge rusher Chop Robinson reports to camp carrying roughly ten added pounds of muscle.
Practice two runs as flagged - the hardest and longest of the week - with a shift toward individual and 11-on-11 work over 7-on-7 drills and an explicit emphasis on cutting penalties this season.

First public practice of camp runs as part of the NFL's 'Back Together Weekend,' free and open to fans, showcasing Malik Willis and rookies Kadyn Proctor, Chris Johnson, Jacob Rodriguez, and Chris Bell.

threads.title: Miami summer restaurant wave
threads.current_state: Miami Spice's discounted dining season ($40 lunch/brunch, $50-65 dinner prix fixe) kicks off today and runs through September 30. Crisppi's opened a second Miami location in West Miami (a former Pollo Tropical drive-thru on SW Eighth Street) and Flight West opened in South Miami pairing live-fire cooking with an ambitious whiskey program, joining Manoli, Redhead Burger, Star Burger, and Stephen Starr's Slim's among this summer's arrivals. Fall list remains: Genghis Cohen, Royale Pizza Napoletana, Miami Slice, Levain Bakery.

Manoli opens; fall 2026 anticipated list published.

threads.title: 2026 CRE capital markets under pressure
threads.current_state: South Florida commercial sales volume remains down 13% year over year, and the summer's biggest single industrial deal - Waste Management's $379M purchase of 146 acres in Medley - was 96% seller-financed. Rents in Miami's most sought-after office towers broke $200/sqft in July, anchored by Peter Thiel's family office paying a record $250/sqft at 830 Brickell. The citywide full-service asking rent has now also hit an all-time high of $63.63/sqft, up 2.0% quarter over quarter and 6.3% year over year, with 429,712 sqft of positive absorption in Q2 - still the highest average of any US market by most measures, though exact figures vary $59.66-67.12/sqft depending on methodology.

timeline.summary: First tracked: CBRE Q2 update shows deal volume down 24% YoY, construction spending below plan, hiring slowing.
South Florida-specific data surfaces: commercial sales volume down 13% year over year to $5.42B in H1 2026.
Waste Management pays $379M for 146 acres in Medley to build a landfill; $366M of the price, 96%, is seller financing rather than a bank loan.

A LoopNet analysis of roughly 5,000 office listings finds Miami's average asking rent, $59.66/sq ft, now the highest in the US, ahead of New York's $50.56 - a sign of how much capital has relocated to Miami since 2020 even as deal volume overall stays soft.

Pebb Capital buys a Miami Beach office building with $69M in ACORE Capital financing; a Wynwood commercial parcel sells for $24.5M, the region's priciest trade that week - real transactions behind the aggregate rent data.
Rents in Miami's top towers cross $200/sqft for the first time, anchored by Peter Thiel's family office paying a record $250/sqft at 830 Brickell; Q2 leasing citywide up nearly 45% YoY to 1.3M sq ft.
Citywide full-service asking rent hits an all-time high of $63.63/sqft (+2.0% QoQ, +6.3% YoY), with 429,712 sqft of positive Q2 absorption.

threads.title: Miami Marine Stadium's restoration referendum
threads.current_state: Miami voters decide Marine Stadium's future in an August 18 referendum (Referendum #172) on a 40-year management deal with Global Spectrum/Oak View Group and local partner Breakwater Hospitality. Under the deal, the city keeps 93% of event revenue and 85% of sponsorship income, with up to $10M toward restoration up front, followed by a separate $65-85M restoration bond. Early voting begins tomorrow, August 3, and runs through August 16; partial pile and seating repairs are already underway with county and state grant money.

timeline.summary: First tracked: City Commission approved the Global Spectrum/Oak View management deal in February; referendum set for August 18; partial restoration already underway.

Additional detail surfaces: the deal is formally Referendum #172, with early voting set for August 3-16 and a specified revenue split (93% events, 85% sponsorship) plus a separate $65-85M restoration bond beyond the initial $10M.
Early voting confirmed to begin tomorrow, August 3; the adjacent Seaquarium site's marina redevelopment surfaces as a related but separate decision over the same stretch of public waterfront.

threads.title: Miami Seaquarium's marina redevelopment
threads.current_state: Miami-Dade County and Terra Group/David Martin have applied to build what could be the county's largest marina at the shuttered Seaquarium site on Virginia Key - 325 slips (about 90 for yachts over 80ft), a 500-boat dry stack, a fuel depot, and floating docks extending partway across the channel. Environmental regulators have raised concerns about wetlands, coral, and water quality; if approved, demolition could start late 2026 with an opening target around 2029. Martin bought the Seaquarium's lease for $22.5M after the park closed in October 2025 after 70 years, and plans to keep an aquarium plus add a Fishermen's Village-style restaurant district and public baywalk.

timeline.summary: First tracked: marina application details surface - 325 slips, 500-boat dry stack, fuel depot; environmental review pending; potential late-2026 groundbreaking.
